A transformer combines attention with position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections, and normalization. Attention lets each position read weighted combinations of other positions’ value vectors. The weights come from query–key scores computed from the current representations using learned projections. A high weight says where information enters that computation; it does not identify a high-entropy token or guarantee semantic importance. (Vaswani et al., 2023)
The architecture and the training objective are separate choices. The original transformer had an encoder and a decoder for translation. Here I focus on a decoder-only autoregressive language model: read a prefix, produce a distribution for the next token, append a token, repeat. 1706.03762⁠ (Vaswani et al., 2023) . There is also a more recent blog post that goes beyond just a simple GPT-like architecture (probably a bit more updated with Kimi, Gated Delta Rule, et al.)

Token IDs select rows from an embedding table. Position information enters through positional embeddings or an operation such as rotary position encoding. Each block updates those representations through attention and a feed-forward network. A final projection produces one logit per vocabulary item. GPT-2 report, §2.3

For one attention head, with queries Q, keys K, values V, and key width d_k:
$$\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+C\right)V,
\qquad
C_{t,j}=\begin{cases}0&j\leq t,\\-\infty&j>t.\end{cases}$$
The softmax runs across key positions. The causal mask $C$ prevents position $t$ from reading future tokens. Multiple heads use separate projections, then combine their outputs. 1706.03762⁠ (Vaswani et al., 2023) 
For a batch of $B$ sequences with $T$ input positions and vocabulary $\mathcal V$, logits have shape $B\times T\times |\mathcal V|$. Let $y_{b,t}=x_{b,t+1}$ be the target after input position $t$, and let $m_{b,t}$ equal one exactly where that target should contribute to training. With $N_{\mathrm{sup}}=\sum_{b,t}m_{b,t}>0$:
a batchA batch can contain padding or targets excluded from supervision, so the denominator counts supervised positions. For example, sequences with three and one supervised targets contribute four terms in total. Using the padded batch size would change the loss scale when padding changes.
Training supplies the actual prefix at every position. The causal mask permits all these next-token predictions in one forward pass. During generation, each sampled token becomes part of the next prefix.

=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sup}}}
\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{t=1}^{T}

memory limitations.
See also: state-space models, Karpathy’s linked thread.
A transformer uses memory for weights, temporary activations, and, during cached decoding, previous keys and values. Dense attention over a sequence of length $T$ computes $T^2$ query–key scores per head. Implementations can avoid storing the complete score matrix; that changes memory traffic and storage without removing all those interactions. 2009.06732⁠ (Tay et al., 2022) 
For an ordinary uncompressed KV cache with $L$ layers, $B$ sequences of length $T$, $h_{\mathrm{KV}}$ key/value heads, equal key and value width $d_h$, and $s$ bytes per element:
$$\operatorname{KVBytes}=2BLTh_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hs.$$
The factor of two counts keys and values. Under these assumptions, doubling the context doubles cache storage. Grouped-query attention reduces the number of KV heads; compression and offloading change what is stored or where it lives. The serving bottleneck also depends on how quickly hardware can move those bytes. 2403.14123⁠ (Gholami et al., 2024) 
inference.
Prefill processes a prompt and builds its KV cache. Decode extends the sequence, usually one token per iteration. Disaggregated serving runs those stages on separate workers, which requires transferring or sharing the cache between them.
sampling
Given finite logits $z_i$ over vocabulary $\mathcal V$, the base distribution is
$$p_i=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal V}e^{z_j}}.$$
A sampler changes this distribution before drawing a token. The following definitions describe individual operations. Their composition needs an explicit order.
temperature
For $\tau>0$:
$$p_i^{(\tau)}=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}.$$
Let $A=\{i:z_i=\max_j z_j\}$ be the set of tied maxima. Then

$$p_i=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal V}e^{z_j}}.$$
A sampler changes this distribution before drawing a token. The following definitions describe individual operations. Their composition needs an explicit order.
temperature
For $\tau>0$:
$$p_i^{(\tau)}=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}.$$
Let $A=\{i:z_i=\max_j z_j\}$ be the set of tied maxima. Then
$$\lim_{\tau\to0^+}p_i^{(\tau)}=\frac{\mathbf1[i\in A]}{|A|},
\qquad
\lim_{\tau\to\infty}p_i^{(\tau)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal V|}.$$
The low-temperature limit is uniform over exact ties. An implementation’s greedy mode can choose one tied token through a separate tie-breaking rule.
For fixed finite logits, entropy is nondecreasing with temperature:
$$H(p^{(\tau)})=-\sum_i p_i^{(\tau)}\log p_i^{(\tau)},
\qquad
\frac{dH}{d\tau}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{p^{(\tau)}}(z)}{\tau^3}\geq0.$$
This follows by differentiating the softmax partition function. It concerns the next-token distribution before any truncation. It does not establish the quality or diversity of complete answers.
top-k
Choose a deterministic ordering for probability ties, and let $S_k$ contain the first $k$ tokens in descending probability order. Keep those tokens and renormalize:
$$p_i^{(k)}=\frac{p_i\mathbf1[i\in S_k]}{\sum_{j\in S_k}p_j}.$$
Exactly $k$ candidates survive under this definition. A threshold implementation that keeps every token tied with the kth token can retain more. The parameter fixes a count even when probability is distributed unevenly across those candidates.
top-p (nucleus)
Write the descending probabilities as p_{(1)},\ldots,p_{(|\mathcal V|)}. For a mass threshold \rho\in(0,1], choose
k_\rho=\min\left\{$k$:\sum_{j=1}^{k}p_{(j)}\geq\rho\right\}.

Exactly $k$ candidates survive under this definition. A threshold implementation that keeps every token tied with the kth token can retain more. The parameter fixes a count even when probability is distributed unevenly across those candidates.
top-p (nucleus)
Write the descending probabilities as p_{(1)},\ldots,p_{(|\mathcal V|)}. For a mass threshold \rho\in(0,1], choose
k_\rho=\min\left\{$k$:\sum_{j=1}^{k}p_{(j)}\geq\rho\right\}.
Retain the first $k_\rho$ tokens, including the token that crosses the threshold, and renormalize. The number retained changes with the distribution. A direct implementation sorts the vocabulary; this is an implementation choice, not a requirement that every sampler use a full sort. (Holtzman et al., 2020) 1904.09751⁠ (Holtzman et al., 2020) 
min-p
For a relative threshold $m\in[0,1]$, retain
$$S_m=\{i:p_i\geq m\max_j p_j\}.$$
Then renormalize on $S_m$. At $m=0$, every token survives; at $m=1$, only the maxima survive. For positive $m$ after temperature scaling, the same condition can be written without computing probabilities:
$$z_i-z_{\max}\geq\tau\log m.$$
This makes the interaction with temperature explicit. Increasing $\tau$ widens the allowed logit gap for fixed $m$.
Nguyen et al. report gains from min-p, including at high temperatures. (Nguyen et al., 2025) A subsequent 2506.13681⁠ (Schaeffer et al., 2025)  disputes the claimed advantage after checking the evaluations and matching hyperparameter searches. The relative probability floor defines the method; superiority over top-p remains an empirical claim to evaluate for the model, task, and tuning budget.

A serving library’s sampler determines its order, renormalization, and tie rules. Check the deployed version before assuming a pipeline. The vLLM sampler source is an implementation reference whose contents can change.

KV
A KV cache stores the key and value representations from earlier positions at each cached layer. In a causal model, appending a token leaves those earlier representations unchanged, so the next query can reuse them. Caching avoids recomputing the prefix; the query still has to attend over the available keys and values.
Mooncake organizes serving around this cache and prefill and decode disaggregation. Its cache transfers and placement policies are system-level choices. (Qin et al., 2024)

Prefill streams KV one layer at a time. Before layer \ell runs attention, the node waits for that layer’s cached prefix to arrive and starts loading layer \ell+1; after attention, the messenger ships layer \ell to the decode node. Overlap hides much of the transfer time while each layer has enough computation to cover it. The first load and final transfer still add latency. A large cached prefix leaves less compute to hide communication; congestion or a slower link can make transfers dominate. 2407.00079⁠ (Qin et al., 2024) .

next-token prediction.
Ordinary autoregressive sampling draws one token from the distribution conditioned on the existing prefix:
$$x_{t+1}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t}),
\qquad
p_\theta(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).$$
There is no explicit lookahead over future token sequences in this procedure. Beam search and Speculative decoding add different mechanisms for exploring or proposing continuations.

multi-token prediction.
Gloeckle et al. train several output prediction heads on a shared trunk. Each head predicts a different future offset from the same prefix representation. These heads are distinct from the attention heads inside a transformer block. (Gloeckle et al., 2024) 2404.19737⁠ (Gloeckle et al., 2024) 
For a sequence of length $T$, let $q_{\theta,r}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t})$ be the distribution from offset head $r$. One token-averaged objective is
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{MTP}}
=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{MTP}}}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sum_{t=1}^{T-r}
\log q_{\theta,r}(x_{t+r}\mid x_{\leq t}),
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{MTP}}=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(T-r),\quad 1\leq n<T.$$
All heads must contribute gradients to the shared trunk. Write its sequence of hidden states as $h=f_{\theta_{\mathrm{trunk}}}(x)$, and let $\ell_r$ be the loss from head $r$. The chain rule gives
$$\nabla_{\theta_{\mathrm{trunk}}}\sum_r\ell_r
=\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial\theta_{\mathrm{trunk}}}\right)^\top
\sum_r\nabla_h\ell_r.$$
Detaching the trunk output without returning these accumulated gradients would prevent the head losses from training the trunk.
Ordinary next-token inference can use the first output head. The additional heads can also propose tokens for self-speculative decoding, followed by verification. Predicting future offsets independently does not make their product the model’s autoregressive joint distribution.

Byte-Latent Transformer
2412.09871⁠ (Pagnoni et al., 2024)  models raw bytes through three stages: a local encoder groups byte representations into patches, a larger transformer processes the patch sequence, and a local decoder predicts bytes. Patch boundaries depend on a smaller model’s next-byte entropy estimates. Predictable stretches can use longer patches, reducing the number of positions processed by the large transformer.
This removes a fixed subword tokenizer. The byte representation, patching rule, and local encoder/decoder still determine how text enters and leaves the model.
Feynman-Kac
2306.03081⁠ (Lew et al., 2023)  describe generation as a Markov chain over token strings, reweighted by nonnegative potentials. (Lew et al., 2023) The transition proposes a continuation; the potential scores that transition for the target task.

Let s_0 be the initial string, $M_t(s_t\mid s_{t-1})$ a normalized transition kernel, and $G_t(s_{t-1},s_t)\geq0$ a potential. Use a fixed horizon $H$ here to make termination explicit. An EOS-terminated string is absorbing, with a self-transition and potential one on subsequent steps. The path target is
$$\gamma_H(s_{1:H})=\prod_{t=1}^{H}M_t(s_t\mid s_{t-1})G_t(s_{t-1},s_t),
\qquad
\pi_H(s_{1:H})=\frac{\gamma_H(s_{1:H})}{Z_H},
\qquad
Z_H=\sum_{s_{1:H}}\gamma_H(s_{1:H}).$$
This requires $0<Z_H<\infty$. The endpoint distribution is the marginal of $\pi_H$ at $s_H$. Sequences that have not reached EOS by $H$ remain truncated prefixes unless the target explicitly excludes them. An unbounded construction needs assumptions about termination and integrability before taking a limit.
A simple bootstrap particle approximation proceeds as follows. This is the standard with-replacement construction, separate from Lew et al.’s branching and without-replacement algorithm. Doucet and Johansen’s particle-filter tutorial

Start with $N$ copies of $s_0$, each with normalized weight $W_0^{(i)}=1/N$.
At each $t\in\{1,\ldots,H\}$, draw ancestor indices $A_t^{(i)}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(W_{t-1})$, then propose $S_t^{(i)}\sim M_t(\cdot\mid S_{t-1}^{(A_t^{(i)})})$.
Set $g_t^{(i)}=G_t(S_{t-1}^{(A_t^{(i)})},S_t^{(i)})$, and normalize $W_t^{(i)}=g_t^{(i)}/\sum_jg_t^{(j)}$.
If every weight is zero, this particle population has failed. It cannot be normalized. At the horizon, use $\sum_i W_H^{(i)}\delta_{S_H^{(i)}}$ as the endpoint approximation.

Resampling favors prefixes that have accumulated weight. Finite populations can lose useful continuations, especially when constraints only become informative near the end. The weighted empirical measure is an approximation; its normalized probabilities are not generally unbiased.
With finite integrable potentials, the bootstrap normalizer estimate is
$$\widehat Z_H=\prod_{t=1}^{H}\left(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}g_t^{(i)}\right).$$

Under the stated multinomial resampling scheme it is unbiased for $Z_H$. A population that reaches zero total weight contributes $\widehat Z_H=0$.
